title: How a MOSFET switches: gate charge, Rds(on), and thermal limits
summary: Explorer-style walkthrough: pick a gate-drive voltage and a load current, then read Qg, Rds(on), conduction loss, and temperature rise from the tables.

blocks.eyebrow: Explorer — gate voltage × load (no live widgets; tables stand in)
blocks.title: Dial Vgs and load current, then read the heat
blocks.body: Treat the checklists below like sliders: pick one gate-drive voltage and one load current. The tables and stats show what that choice does to gate charge, on-resistance, conduction loss, and a rough ΔT. This is an illustrative explorer, not a datasheet substitute.

items.label: Knob A — gate drive (4.5 / 7 / 10 V examples)
Knob B — load current (2 / 5 / 10 A examples)

blocks.heading: Slider A — choose gate-drive voltage (pick one mentally)

items.label: Vgs = 4.5 V (logic-level drive)
items.detail: Works if the part is characterized there; Rds(on) is usually worse than at 10 V.

items.label: Vgs = 7 V (middle drive)
items.detail: Common compromise on 5–12 V rails with a gate driver.

items.label: Vgs = 10 V (classic strong drive)
items.detail: Often the Rds(on) number glowing on the front page of the datasheet.

blocks.heading: Slider B — choose load current (pick one mentally)

items.label: Id = 2 A continuous
items.detail: Light load — conduction loss usually small unless Rds(on) is high.

items.label: Id = 5 A continuous
items.detail: Medium — where many hobby switching stages live.

items.label: Id = 10 A continuous
items.detail: Heavy for a tiny package — heat dominates the story.

nodes.title: 1. Gate charge at your Vgs
nodes.detail: Qg (and related Qgd) set how hard the driver must push to switch in time.

nodes.title: 2. Rds(on) at that Vgs and temperature
nodes.detail: On-resistance falls as Vgs rises (within ratings) and rises as the die heats.

nodes.title: 3. Conduction loss ≈ Id² × Rds(on)
nodes.detail: Steady on-state heat. Switching loss is extra when you chop fast — noted below, not fully modeled here.

nodes.title: 4. ΔT ≈ Ploss × RθJA (or RθJC+heatsink path)
nodes.detail: If ΔT pushes you past T_j(max), you need copper, airflow, a bigger FET, or less current.

blocks.heading: Example gate charge vs Vgs (illustrative mid-size N-FET)
rows: Typical with a small gate driver
blocks.caption: Numbers are teaching examples. Real parts vary widely — read the Qg vs Vgs curve.

blocks.heading: Example Rds(on) and conduction loss at 25 °C
blocks.caption: P ≈ Id² × Rds(on). Cross your two slider picks to read a cell.

blocks.heading: Thermal read-out (example RθJA ≈ 40 °C/W on 1 in² copper)
rows: OK if switching loss is modest
Watch margins; copper and airflow matter
Resize FET, add sink, or cut current
blocks.caption: Add switching loss when you PWM hard. Hot Rds(on) is higher than the 25 °C row — derate.

blocks.heading: How to run one explorer pass
items: Pick a Vgs row in the gate-charge and Rds tables (slider A).
Pick an Id column (slider B) and read conduction loss.
Drop that loss into the thermal table (or multiply by your own Rθ).
Ask: is Tj still inside rating with room for switching loss and hot Rds(on)?

blocks.title: What this explorer under-models
blocks.body: Switching loss (~½·Vds·Id·(tr+tf)·f plus gate-drive loss Qg·Vdrive·f) is not fully simulated here. Fast PWM at high Vds can dominate heat even when Id²R looks fine. Treat the tables as the conduction half of the story.

blocks.heading: Explorer drill
blocks.prompt: You set Vgs = 4.5 V and Id = 10 A on the example tables. What should worry you first?
options: Conduction loss ~1.2 W and a soft thermal margin before switching loss
The FET cannot turn on at any current
blocks.explanation: At 4.5 V / 10 A the example conduction loss is about 1.2 W — already a meaningful ΔT before you add switching loss and hot Rds(on).

columns.name: Raise Vgs (within abs max)
columns.detail: Often lowers Rds(on) and conduction loss; raises Qg and gate-drive effort.

columns.name: Raise Id
columns.detail: Loss scales with Id² in conduction. Thermal headroom shrinks fast.

blocks.heading: Next
blocks.body: Open a real datasheet. Find Rds(on) vs Vgs, Qg, and thermal resistance. Re-run the same two-slider pass with the part you will actually buy.
